title: What is known about 1RB1LF_1RC0RA_0RD1RA_1RE1LA_0LA---_1RF0LD
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB1LF_1RC0RA_0RD1RA_1RE1LA_0LA---_1RF0LD.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open. The left end runs a binary decrement over bits separated by blocks of 10 (proved in Lean for one to three borrows); a halt needs the head in A on four 0s in a row (proved in Lean), which the counter makes only when two neighbouring blocks are empty at once. Perturbing the block lengths of a real configuration makes the machine halt, so non-halting depends on the arithmetic of the lengths; the rewriting rule for an empty block is not yet decoded.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (E1); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 85,032 cells have been visited and 42,517 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: No halt in the first 7.44×10<sup>18</sup> steps (exact macro run)
claims.text: A macro simulator (blocks of 6 cells, long runs of equal blocks crossed in one go; exact: every macro step is a run of the machine, counted step for step) ran from blank tape to step 7,445,689,167,405,862,579 without a halt. At this block size it gives the same state, head position and tape as the direct simulator after 2,000,010,627 steps. This is a bounded run and says nothing about later steps.

claims.title: Growth shape: exp/sqrt
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.542). Right of the start it grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.1).

claims.title: The sweeps
claims.text: Eight shift rules over (10)^n, (01)^n and (011)^n, for all n and any tapes around (one copy by rfl, all copies by TM.cross_r / TM.cross_l).

claims.title: Right-end events to 4.5·10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: A C run to 5·109 steps, sampled each time the tape grows on the right (62 times): a list of blocks a^x (a = 10) separated by 1^4 0; block j from the right loses 2j copies of a from one event to the next, and fresh leftmost blocks have length 2m−3.

claims.title: The binary decrement at the left end
claims.text: At a left-end visit the tape is A> 0 (10)^x b1 (10)^y1 b2 (10)^y2 … with one-cell bits. With the lowest set bit first, second or third, one visit clears it, sets the bits below it, takes one copy from the block after it and adds two copies to the first block, for all lengths.

claims.title: A halt needs four 0s in a row
claims.text: Four steps before any halting configuration the head is in state A on 0 0 0 0 1 (E is entered only from D on 0, D next to a 1 only from C on 0, C only from B on 0, B only from A on 0).

claims.title: Runs of zeros stay short
claims.text: A run of zeros grows for good only when B reads 1 1 0^r. In 109 steps from blank tape a run of three zeros ((10)^k 11 000 (10)^m) is made 37 times and a run of four never.

claims.title: Non-halting depends on the block lengths
claims.text: Replacing the block lengths of the real configuration at the right-end event of step 173,780,460 by random ones makes the machine halt: 4 of 100 trials with lengths in [1, 60] within 2·107 steps, 3 of 300 with lengths in [5, 300] of the real parity within 5·107. Each halt comes from two neighbouring blocks running out together ((10)^x 0 0 0 (10)^y). So no tape language that forgets the lengths can be closed and halt-free.

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not known. It halts exactly if two neighbouring blocks are ever empty together with zero bits around them; the rule that rewrites the list when the borrow meets an empty block is not decoded, so this is not yet a question about a map.

claims.title: Related holdouts
claims.text: The same table as 1RB0RE_0RC1RE_1RD1LE_0LE---_1RA1LF_1RF0LC up to renaming, started in another state; no common configuration in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps of each. explainer.lede: Nobody knows. The left end of the tape is a binary counter: one-cell bits between blocks of 10s, and every time a bit is cleared the block after it pays one copy. It can only halt if two neighbouring blocks run out at the same time.

facts.text: No halt in the C simulator.
A halt needs the head in A on four 0s in a row (Lean).
One visit of the left end decrements the counter, proved for one to three borrows.
Perturbed block lengths halt in about 2% of trials: the lengths matter.

sections.heading: A binary counter that pays with blocks
html: Write a for 10. Each time the head reaches a new cell at the left end the tape reads
A> 0 a^x  b1 a^y1  b2 a^y2  …  bk a^yk  tail
with single-cell bits b (0 or 1) between blocks. One visit of the left end is one binary decrement (b1 is the lowest bit):

• the lowest bit that is 1 becomes 0 and the bits below it become 1;
  • the block just after that bit loses one copy;
  • the first block gains two copies.

So the block after bit j pays one copy every 2j visits. When every bit is 0 the borrow runs out to the right end (the rare events on the slow side of the tape) and the counter starts again with a new first block. When the borrow meets an empty block the list is rewritten, blocks are split and merged; that rule is not decoded yet.

sections.heading: Four zeros in a row
html: The machine stops only on E reading 1. Tracing back four steps (proved in Lean): E comes only from D on a 0, D next to a 1 only from C on a 0, C only from B on a 0, B only from A on a 0. So a halt needs the head in state A on 0 0 0 0 1: four blank cells inside the written tape.

The counter's zeros come alone or in pairs. Two empty blocks side by side with zero bits around them give a^x 0 0 0 a^y, four zeros in a row with the last 0 of the block, and that is how a halt would happen.

Is it avoided because of the shape of the tape, or because of the numbers? When the block lengths of a real configuration are replaced by random ones (keeping the shape, even keeping every length odd as the real ones are), about 2% of the runs halt within 107–108 steps, always by two neighbouring blocks running out together. The real lengths never do. So a proof that it never halts has to follow the arithmetic of the lengths; a closed tape language that forgets them cannot work.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.542). Right of the start it grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.1).
After 109 steps the tape spans 85,032 cells (56,027 left of the start, 102 right), with a density of 1s of 0.5.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

sections.heading: Related machines
html: Other holdouts of the list of 608 that are tied to this one. The comparison of tables is exact; everything about runs was checked on the first 107 steps of each machine and is an observation, not a proof (holdouts/related.py, holdouts/related.json).

Same table as the machines below, started in another state. Renaming the states as shown turns this machine's table into the other one, the halting transition included. The other machine starts in its own state A, which is not this machine's A: its run from blank tape is the run of this table started in another state. These are different runs: in the first 107 steps of each, no configuration of this machine's run occurs in any of the others, even up to a shift of the tape. So each of these holdouts is its own halting question, and settling one does not settle another.

  • 1RB1LC_0LC---_1RE1LD_1RD0LA_1RF0RC_0RA1RC: rename A→C, B→E, C→F, D→A, E→B, F→D; it is this table started in state D

summary: A binary counter whose bits sit between blocks of 10s, each block paying one copy when its bit is cleared; a halt needs two neighbouring blocks to run out together, which depends on the block lengths themselves.
